items.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: a guy who I befriended named Johnny Mandel

ctx.x: Interesting. Were you able, at this point, we’re talking about mid 50s to late 50s, you’re actually making a living doing this? Kind of?

I have to confess that I had some help from my family. I was making a living but I was doing better than if I was just playing the music with my family’s help. Because the only white guys I know that were making a living, there were very few white musicians who © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

actually made a living just playing jazz. In other words, guys like Al Cohn and Johnny Mandel, a whole school of guys, they were doing commercial work. Arranging or playing all kinds of studio dates. They became studio musicians. There was just a handful, like Stan Getz and Zoot, who didn’t want, I mean he was the exception because he was a true Bohemian or whatever they called them.

items.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It was Dick Katz was playing piano, he was going, we became very friendly after that

ctx.x: Then they wouldn’t even let me in because I hadn’t had a classical grounding, the fact that I had played in all these bands meant nothing to them, I had to camp outside the school for two days. I’d said, “I’m just gonna sit myself on the doorstep and not leave, until you let me in,” they let me in to get rid of me. Then I discovered there was another two jazz musicians in there, but they were, you know, good classical musicians. It was Dick Katz was playing piano, he was going, we became very friendly after that…
Was John Lewis there at the time?
